summary.title: Cognitive load is what matters
summary.one_liner: Learn to judge code quality by the mental effort (cognitive load) it forces on developers, and how common practices like deep modules, early returns, self-describing codes and fewer abstractions reduce it.
keywords: how to make code easier to understand
takeaways: Confusion while reading code is a measurable cost, caused by excess working-memory load; the goal is to reduce extraneous (presentation-caused) cognitive load.
Prefer deep modules with simple interfaces over many shallow classes, and prefer flat, early-return control flow with named intermediate variables.
Avoid over-applying DRY, premature abstraction, heavy framework coupling and layered architectures that add indirection without practical payoff.
Use self-describing string codes instead of numeric status mappings, and keep a monolith with isolated modules until separate deployment is truly needed.
Limit language features and choices so that future readers do not have to reconstruct the author's reasoning.
summary.summary: The essay argues that developers should judge code by the confusion and working-memory load it causes, rather than by fashionable best practices like short methods, strict SRP, microservices, DRY, or layered architecture. It explains a simple model of cognitive load (roughly four chunks in working memory) and walks through concrete code examples: complex conditionals, nested ifs versus early returns, inheritance chains, and shallow versus deep modules drawn from John Ousterhout's work. Further sections use anecdotes from the author's projects, a startup's microservice split, a C++ engineer's experience, and HTTP status code mapping to illustrate the points. Code snippets are in pseudo-code and Java-like syntax, with emoji markers for estimated load levels.
